SECURITY INTERESTS IN INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY — WHERE A LIEN ON A PATENT OR COPYRIGHT IS PERFECTED — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Northsound Avionics, Inc. · Harbor Line Capital, LLC

SECURITY INTERESTS IN INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY — WHAT THIS INFORMATION SHEET COVERS
This information sheet describes the law that decides where a lien on intellectual property has to be recorded, and what happens between two people who claim the same intellectual property. It is written for a transaction in which Northsound Avionics, Inc. grants Harbor Line Capital, LLC a security interest in U.S. Patent No. 7,123,456 and the software copyrights in the FlightLog source code.

The question it addresses is a narrow one, and it is not the question most intellectual-property material asks. The usual question is who owns a patent, a copyright, a mark or a trade secret, and what the owner can do about a copier. The question here is different: intellectual property is also personal property that can be pledged to a lender, and two separate recording systems — California’s Division 9 filing system run by the Secretary of State, and the federal registers kept by the United States Copyright Office and the United States Patent and Trademark Office — each claim some part of the subject. Which one governs is not the same answer for patents, for registered copyrights, and for unregistered copyrights.

What follows states the statutory text of California Commercial Code Division 9 and of the federal Copyright, Patent and Bankruptcy Acts, and the holdings of the two published Ninth Circuit opinions that construe them. It does not evaluate Northsound Avionics, Inc.’s or Harbor Line Capital, LLC’s transaction, does not say where any particular filing should be made, and does not predict how a court would rule on any set of facts.

INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY SITS IN ARTICLE 9’S RESIDUAL COLLATERAL CATEGORY (CAL. COM. CODE § 9102(A)(42))
California’s Division 9 sorts personal-property collateral into named types, and defines the residual type, "general intangible," by subtraction rather than by description. Section 9102(a)(42) says the term means any personal property, including things in action, other than a closed list of other collateral types — accounts, chattel paper, commercial tort claims, deposit accounts, documents, goods, instruments, investment property, letter-of-credit rights, letters of credit, money, and oil, gas or other minerals before extraction — and adds that the term includes payment intangibles and software. Patents, copyrights, trademarks and trade secrets appear nowhere on the list of exclusions. Construing the predecessor of this definition, the Ninth Circuit stated flatly that Article 9 applies to general intangibles, a term that includes intellectual property. That categorisation is what brings U.S. Patent No. 7,123,456 and the software copyrights in the FlightLog source code within Division 9 in the first place, and it is why the rest of this sheet is about which filing office applies rather than whether Division 9 applies at all.

THE DEFAULT: A FINANCING STATEMENT MUST BE FILED (CAL. COM. CODE § 9310(A))
Division 9’s starting point is that perfection requires a filing. Section 9310(a) provides that, except as otherwise provided in subdivision (b) and in subdivision (b) of section 9312, a financing statement must be filed to perfect all security interests and agricultural liens. Every departure from that rule for intellectual property has to be found somewhere else — in section 9310(b)’s own list, in the federal-preemption provision of section 9109, or in section 9311, which is where a federal filing system enters the analysis. Nothing in section 9310 itself carves out patents, copyrights, trademarks or trade secrets.

DIVISION 9 STEPS BACK WHERE FEDERAL LAW PREEMPTS IT (CAL. COM. CODE § 9109(C)(1))
Division 9 contains its own instruction about when it yields to federal law. Section 9109(c) states that the division does not apply to the extent that either of two conditions is satisfied, the first being that a statute, regulation or treaty of the United States preempts the division. This is the provision that opens the question this sheet is about: whether the Copyright Act or the Patent Act is such a statute, and if so how far the step-back reaches. The section supplies the trigger; it does not itself identify any federal statute as preemptive, and it leaves the scope of any step-back — "to the extent that" — to be worked out statute by statute.

COMPLIANCE WITH A QUALIFYING FEDERAL STATUTE REPLACES THE FINANCING STATEMENT (CAL. COM. CODE § 9311(A)(1), (B))
Section 9311 supplies the narrower of Division 9’s two deferrals. Subdivision (a) provides that, except as otherwise provided in subdivision (d), the filing of a financing statement is not necessary or effective to perfect a security interest in property subject to a statute, regulation or treaty of the United States whose requirements for a security interest obtaining priority over the rights of a lien creditor with respect to the property preempt section 9310(a). Subdivision (b) then states the consequence: compliance with the requirements of such a statute for obtaining priority over the rights of a lien creditor is equivalent to the filing of a financing statement under the division, and a security interest in property subject to such a statute may be perfected only by compliance with those requirements. Two features of the text do the work in intellectual-property disputes. The federal statute must speak to priority over a lien creditor, not merely provide a place to record something; and where it does, the state filing is not merely unnecessary but ineffective.

A COPYRIGHT SECURITY INTEREST IS A "TRANSFER OF COPYRIGHT OWNERSHIP" (17 U.S.C. § 101)
The Copyright Act’s definitional section is what connects a lender’s lien to the Act’s recording machinery. Section 101 defines a transfer of copyright ownership as an assignment, mortgage, exclusive license, or any other conveyance, alienation, or hypothecation of a copyright or of any of the exclusive rights comprised in a copyright, whether or not it is limited in time or place of effect, but not including a nonexclusive license. The words "mortgage" and "hypothecation" are the ones that matter here: a security interest granted by Northsound Avionics, Inc. to Harbor Line Capital, LLC in a copyright is a transfer of copyright ownership as the Act uses that phrase, which is why the Act’s recordation section, section 205, reaches it at all. The Patent Act contains no comparable definitional sentence.

RECORDATION IN THE COPYRIGHT OFFICE, AND WHY REGISTRATION IS A PRECONDITION TO CONSTRUCTIVE NOTICE (17 U.S.C. § 205(A), (C))
Section 205(a) provides that any transfer of copyright ownership or other document pertaining to a copyright may be recorded in the Copyright Office if the document filed for recordation bears the actual signature of the person who executed it, or if it is accompanied by a sworn or official certification that it is a true copy of the original, signed document. Recording is permitted, not commanded. What recording accomplishes is set out in subdivision (c): recordation of a document in the Copyright Office gives all persons constructive notice of the facts stated in the recorded document, but only if two conditions are met — the document or material attached to it specifically identifies the work so that, after indexing by the Register of Copyrights, it would be revealed by a reasonable search under the title or registration number of the work, and registration has been made for the work. The second condition is the one that splits this area in two. Where the underlying work is unregistered, recording a document about it in the Copyright Office produces no constructive notice at all.

PRIORITY BETWEEN TWO CONFLICTING COPYRIGHT TRANSFERS, AND THE NONEXCLUSIVE LICENSEE’S IMMUNITY (17 U.S.C. § 205(D), (E))
Section 205(d) states a race-notice rule built on the constructive-notice mechanism of subdivision (c). As between two conflicting transfers, the one executed first prevails if it is recorded, in the manner required to give constructive notice under subsection (c), within one month after its execution in the United States or within two months after its execution outside the United States, or at any time before recordation in such manner of the later transfer; otherwise the later transfer prevails if recorded first in such manner, and if taken in good faith, for valuable consideration or on the basis of a binding promise to pay royalties, and without notice of the earlier transfer. Because a security interest in a copyright is a transfer of copyright ownership under section 101, two lenders taking liens on the same copyright, or a lender and a later assignee, are two conflicting transfers within this subdivision. Subdivision (e) stands outside the race entirely: a nonexclusive license, whether recorded or not, prevails over a conflicting transfer of copyright ownership if the license is evidenced by a written instrument signed by the owner of the rights licensed or that owner’s duly authorized agent, and if the license was taken before execution of the transfer, or was taken in good faith before recordation of the transfer and without notice of it.

REGISTERED COPYRIGHTS GO TO THE COPYRIGHT OFFICE, UNREGISTERED COPYRIGHTS TO THE STATE FILING OFFICE (IN RE WORLD AUXILIARY POWER CO.)
The Ninth Circuit answered the question of where a copyright lien belongs by splitting it. Applying California’s two step-back provisions, the court stated that under those provisions there can be no question that, when a copyright has been registered, a security interest can be perfected only by recording the transfer in the Copyright Office, and that for registered copyrights the only proper place to file is the Copyright Office. For unregistered copyrights the court reached the opposite result, reasoning that there just is not any way for a secured creditor to preserve a priority in an unregistered copyright by recording anything in the Copyright Office. Its conclusion was that, regarding perfection and priority of security interests in unregistered copyrights, the California Uniform Commercial Code has not stepped back in deference to federal law, and federal law has not preempted the Uniform Commercial Code. The practical shape of the holding is that a single copyright portfolio can require filings in two different offices, and that the line between them moves whenever a work is registered.

THE PATENT ACT’S REGISTER AND ITS RECORDING RULE (35 U.S.C. § 261)
The Patent Act maintains a register but describes it in terms that are wider than the rule attached to it. Section 261 provides that the Patent and Trademark Office shall maintain a register of interests in patents and applications for patents and shall record any document related thereto upon request, and may require a fee therefor. That sentence permits the recording of a security interest; it attaches no consequence to doing so. The consequence appears in a separate, narrower sentence: an interest that constitutes an assignment, grant or conveyance shall be void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee for a valuable consideration, without notice, unless it is recorded in the Patent and Trademark Office within three months from its date or prior to the date of such subsequent purchase or mortgage. The gap between the two sentences — a register open to any document, and a voiding rule that runs only against an "assignment, grant or conveyance" and only in favour of a subsequent "purchaser or mortgagee" — is the whole of the patent question in this area.

A PATENT SECURITY INTEREST IS PERFECTED BY STATE FILING, NOT PTO RECORDING (IN RE CYBERNETIC SERVICES, INC.)
The Ninth Circuit framed the patent question as whether the Patent Act or Article 9 as adopted in California requires the holder of a security interest in a patent to record that interest with the federal Patent and Trademark Office in order to perfect the interest as against a subsequent lien creditor, and answered that neither the Patent Act nor Article 9 so requires, affirming the Bankruptcy Appellate Panel. The reasoning ran through the two limits in the statutory sentence quoted above. On the first, the court concluded that the statute’s text, context and structure, read in the light of Supreme Court precedent, compel the conclusion that a security interest in a patent that does not involve a transfer of the rights of ownership is a "mere license" and is not an "assignment, grant or conveyance" within the meaning of section 261. On the second, the court concluded that the historical definitions of "purchaser or mortgagee," taken in context, establish that Congress was concerned only with providing constructive notice to subsequent parties who take an ownership interest in the patent in question. The disposition followed: the secured parties perfected their security interest in the debtor’s patent by recording it with the California Secretary of State, and had priority over the trustee’s claim because they recorded before the bankruptcy petition was filed. Set against the preceding clause on copyrights, the result is that federal and state filing offices divide the field differently for patents than for registered copyrights.

This information sheet describes the law that decides where a lien on intellectual property has to be recorded, and what happens between two people who claim the same intellectual property. It is written for a transaction in which Northsound Avionics, Inc. grants Harbor Line Capital, LLC a security interest in U.S. Patent No. 7,123,456 and the software copyrights in the FlightLog source code.

The question it addresses is a narrow one, and it is not the question most intellectual-property material asks. The usual question is who owns a patent, a copyright, a mark or a trade secret, and what the owner can do about a copier. The question here is different: intellectual property is also personal property that can be pledged to a lender, and two separate recording systems — California’s Division 9 filing system run by the Secretary of State, and the federal registers kept by the United States Copyright Office and the United States Patent and Trademark Office — each claim some part of the subject. Which one governs is not the same answer for patents, for registered copyrights, and for unregistered copyrights.

What follows states the statutory text of California Commercial Code Division 9 and of the federal Copyright, Patent and Bankruptcy Acts, and the holdings of the two published Ninth Circuit opinions that construe them. It does not evaluate Northsound Avionics, Inc.’s or Harbor Line Capital, LLC’s transaction, does not say where any particular filing should be made, and does not predict how a court would rule on any set of facts.

California’s Division 9 sorts personal-property collateral into named types, and defines the residual type, "general intangible," by subtraction rather than by description. Section 9102(a)(42) says the term means any personal property, including things in action, other than a closed list of other collateral types — accounts, chattel paper, commercial tort claims, deposit accounts, documents, goods, instruments, investment property, letter-of-credit rights, letters of credit, money, and oil, gas or other minerals before extraction — and adds that the term includes payment intangibles and software. Patents, copyrights, trademarks and trade secrets appear nowhere on the list of exclusions. Construing the predecessor of this definition, the Ninth Circuit stated flatly that Article 9 applies to general intangibles, a term that includes intellectual property. That categorisation is what brings U.S. Patent No. 7,123,456 and the software copyrights in the FlightLog source code within Division 9 in the first place, and it is why the rest of this sheet is about which filing office applies rather than whether Division 9 applies at all.

expectedJSON.body: The Ninth Circuit answered the question of where a copyright lien belongs by splitting it. Applying California’s two step-back provisions, the court stated that under those provisions there can be no question that, when a copyright has been registered, a security interest can be perfected only by recording the transfer in the Copyright Office, and that for registered copyrights the only proper place to file is the Copyright Office. For unregistered copyrights the court reached the opposite result, reasoning that there just is not any way for a secured creditor to preserve a priority in an unregistered copyright by recording anything in the Copyright Office. Its conclusion was that, regarding perfection and priority of security interests in unregistered copyrights, the California Uniform Commercial Code has not stepped back in deference to federal law, and federal law has not preempted the Uniform Commercial Code. The practical shape of the holding is that a single copyright portfolio can require filings in two different offices, and that the line between them moves whenever a work is registered.

expectedJSON.body: The Patent Act maintains a register but describes it in terms that are wider than the rule attached to it. Section 261 provides that the Patent and Trademark Office shall maintain a register of interests in patents and applications for patents and shall record any document related thereto upon request, and may require a fee therefor. That sentence permits the recording of a security interest; it attaches no consequence to doing so. The consequence appears in a separate, narrower sentence: an interest that constitutes an assignment, grant or conveyance shall be void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee for a valuable consideration, without notice, unless it is recorded in the Patent and Trademark Office within three months from its date or prior to the date of such subsequent purchase or mortgage. The gap between the two sentences — a register open to any document, and a voiding rule that runs only against an "assignment, grant or conveyance" and only in favour of a subsequent "purchaser or mortgagee" — is the whole of the patent question in this area.

Section 9408(a) provides that, subject to subdivisions (b) and (f), a term in an agreement between an account debtor and a debtor relating to a general intangible — including a contract, permit, license, or franchise — which prohibits, restricts, or requires consent to the assignment or transfer of, or the creation, attachment, or perfection of a security interest in, that general intangible is ineffective to the stated extent. Subdivision (d) then narrows what the secured party gains from that override. Where such a term would have been effective under other law but is ineffective under subdivision (a) or (c), the creation, attachment or perfection of the security interest is subject to a list of rules, two of which bear directly on confidential information: it does not entitle the secured party to use, assign, possess, or have access to any trade secrets or confidential information of the person obligated on the promissory note or the account debtor, and it does not entitle the secured party to enforce the security interest in the general intangible. The lien can attach and be perfected over a contractual prohibition; it does not thereby open the counterparty’s secrets to the lender.
